If you look at other cases that are also to be found in the tabs, you will be able to see that you have the most minute details that are recorded and documented on the scene of the crime once an on-site investigation took place after the event, immediately after the event itself, like the event in Suva Reka and I can't remember the others now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I explain what we've done, although it may be simply a matter of interest. I've drawn from every source that I can accounts coming from the Serb side about Racak and put them chronologically. To explore it with any witness would take a very great deal of time. The majority of the documents come from sources other than this witness's proposed documents but some do come from his 140-odd documents. I mention that now because obviously we'll have to deal with that when I seek to exclude either all his documents or all his documents bar those few, but at some stage an analysis of the documents in chronological order is likely, in the conventional way, to assist but it would simply take far more time than I'm disposed to take on this occasion. We may be able to deal with that material through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn to Izbica, please. You gave evidence about Izbica. Again, of course, you weren't there, were you, ever, or were you? Never there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at tab 69, please, in volume 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just bear with me one minute. I haven't marked it, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a meeting at which you were present? Yes, you were. And we will find --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will find in it -- I've temporarily mislaid my reference, my reference to Izbica.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izbica should not be mentioned because we're dealing with the 17th of February, but perhaps that is possible. Is it tab 69?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those minutes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in case I'm in error. By March of 1999, is it right that both the MUP and the VJ were operating in the Drenica region?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. On or about March 1999.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1998 and 1999, both the police and army were operating all over Kosovo and in Drenica certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Were they acting together?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of them did their own job within the frameworks of their competencies, and in the anti-terrorist activities, yes, they did work together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your evidence about Izbica, does it challenge the fact in any way that the people gathering in Izbica were divided, men from women?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the division of the people gathered there into men and women, I learnt about that from the indictment and from your questions or quotations from parts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But if there's been evidence given to this Court that that's what happened and the men were then massacred, do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have reason to doubt because of the fact, if I recall correctly, that in the indictment it says that the number of civilians was several thousand and that the men were separated from the women, children, and elderly and that they were then executed. So from that context and that wording, it would emerge that in a group of 4 or 5.000 civilians there were just 100 men, which is really illogical, and that lack of logic is something that I'm aware of. But let me remind you that everything the police knows about Izbica it knows from the moment at which on the internet or some television screen a satellite image appeared. So the police did not have any knowledge about what had happened before that in that zone, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the evidence that we have includes evidence of somebody who took photographs at the time. Part of our Exhibit 162, tab 4. Here is a photograph of a man with crutches, or with a crutch. Just have a look at that one as an example to remind us. When you were interviewed as a suspect, you didn't suggest that the victim -- here's another one. Have a look at this one, please, Mr. Nort. Same exhibit. You didn't suggest in interview that these victims were active KLA fighters. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the victims who were found in the, conditionally speaking, freshly dug graves in Izbica on the basis of the photographs. And I think I remember correctly I did not know where the victims had come from in that grave and what the cause of their death was. That was supposed to be the subject of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The investigation has never, if it took place and was conscientious, it was never revealed that these victims -- Mr. Nort, this one, please -- it has never revealed, has it, that people shown, for example, in this photograph were members of the KLA actively fighting, has it? That's how they were found.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I remember correctly, during this testimony, from the documents we have here, we were able to note at least four pieces of highly valuable evidence that at least four persons belonged to the KLA. As far as the others are concerned, their membership in the KLA was neither refuted nor confirmed. But that evidence is related to the victims found in that grave, and that is part of the case file that we saw here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please feel free -- if you want to say now different from what you said in your interview, that all these men were fighting members of the KLA, please do so. Is that your -- is that now your evidence?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I do not wish to say anything that I don't know or I have no information about. Of course I don't want to change my evidence in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll take that one back, please, Mr. Nort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then you lingered on the fact that the graves were individual and not a mass grave. Well, that's the evidence we've heard, that that's how they were dug, that they were all dug at the same time. It's quite clear from your own evidence and from the photograph you looked at, similar to the photographs produced in the Prosecution, that the graves were clearly dug at the same time; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individual graves were dug at the same time, relatively speaking, during the same day, but every person that was buried was buried into an individual grave, and all the individual graves were in one location alone. I did not believe that that was called a mass grave. I believe that to be a graveyard. That is how I understand these concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you in some way critical of the villagers and the bereaved who allocated individual graves to individual bodies? Would you have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. preferred them to be in a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has absolutely nothing to do with what I said. I'm simply speaking about the facts from the site. Of course I would not have preferred to have found a mass grave, and of course I wouldn't like any bodies to have been there. I would have preferred that there had been no war and no terrorism in Kosovo at all, and I regret it deeply that you are trying to portray me as the creator and architect of what happened in Kosovo. Of course it would have never crossed my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to know, as we listen to your evidence about individual graves, what point you're trying to make. But if you're saying that you believe in the dignity of the dead, help me with this: When your authorities exhumed those bodies, what machine did they use?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I really don't know which machine they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An excavator?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot believe that an excavator was used, a machine normally used for digging trenches. There are photographs of the grave, and I -- it would be below everybody's dignity to have used an excavator. I can't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tab 69. It was the right tab. My colleagues were right and I missed the point. Can we look at 69, please. It's on page 2 in the English, and it's at a paragraph beginning with the words "Montenegro," in English. So that will translate to the -- I think the bottom of the first page and over to the second page in your version. I'm not sure. Do you see a passage there, it's about three-quarters of the way down, which says at this MUP staff meeting: "The staff plans to carry out three mopping-up operations in the Podujevo, Dragobilje, and Drenica areas"? Do you see that passage? It's right at the foot of page 1. Because it goes on to say "and has allotted around 4.000 policemen, around 70 policemen of the operative pursuit group, and about 900 police reservists." Do you see that? At the bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regret to say I haven't found it yet. The first page begins, in my version: "The main thrust is towards stopping covert activities." Maybe we are looking at different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... five lines up. "The staff plans to carry out three mopping-up --"

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was looking at a completely different tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to the events at --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to these events that happened in March, we see that the MUP were planning mopping-up operations in the Izbica area. What did you mean by "mopping-up," those of you attending this meeting on the 17th of February?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained more than once that the term "mopping-up" means only mopping up the territory from terrorists. It has several meanings. It means to clear up roads, and it means also sanitisation. But in the context of anti-terrorist actions, what is meant are certain specific anti-terrorist actions that were planned to take place in certain areas. That should not be a problem. Podujevo, Dragobilje and Drenica are three regions in Kosovo that were notorious for the presence and activities of terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suppose the lawful police force in February of 1999 would be using the word "mopping up" to mean arresting wherever possible and only resorting to violence and killing people if absolutely essential. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a certain sense, what you said is correct. The objective is what I have already explained it to be, and the consequences were undesirable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go to your diary next, then, please, at page 98 in the English, which we'll place on the overhead projector, which I think will be -- I'll find it for you. It's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You might like to put these -- if you can, Mr. Nort, if you can put the B/C/S on the overhead projector, as well as the English. I don't know if that's going to be possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you help me? Which tab is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 440. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Binder 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it here. It seems I don't have it in my set.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you have this copy in front of you to save time. What we see on this entry --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we see on this entry, which is for the 21st of May, according to the previous page in English, is an entry that says: "Clearing up the terrain, Izbica." Well, now, what was that all about?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to find it first. Please, I can't find it. Did you say it was page 79?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Item number 2 in the list of --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Clearing up the terrain, Izbica. Criminal offences. Isolation. Return of weapons." What does all that mean?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Under item 2 it doesn't say clearing up the terrain, it says "asanacija," "sanitisation," but I will remind you that I said before that we had found about Izbica through an aerial photograph and that we spent several days looking for that place Izbica. I cannot confirm now that we found it, but it seems that we did. And do you know what "sanitisation" means? You have seen it at the example of Pusto Selo. It implies in this case all that is done in keeping with the law on criminal procedure, that means exhumation, verification of information received, in this case the information was obviously checked, and then all the subsequent steps, exhumations pursuant to the orders of the investigating judge, on-site investigation, post-mortems and everything else that you can find in the case file that I brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is about casualties, people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason Izbica had to be investigated is because it was publicised and aerial photographs were produced by international bodies and you had no choice. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not the truth. There were only two cases in Kosovo when we found out about such things, Izbica and Pusto Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the other 1.500 cases, we found about these cases in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you're -- you're asking us to accept, I take it, that with however many policemen there were on the ground in Kosovo altogether, perhaps 15.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "150.000"] police at the time, and with 100 people dying you needed international assistance to tell you that the crime was committed and then you needed days to find the village. Is that really your position, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that there were never 150.000 policemen. There were 15.000 at the most. And of course we didn't need the international organisations to tell us first. We simply needed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- information, reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... small territory like Kosovo. That can't be right, can it? Who --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that it is true, but it does seem illogical. We were simply unable to find it. There is footage showing journalists searching together with us, and they indeed did. We found the place seven days after we started looking. Approximately seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we move, if we can, please, to page --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is accurate. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should ask you, what does the word "crimes" mean on that -- "criminal offences" mean on that entry? What criminal offences are you referring to there if it's only asanacija, sanitisation, that you're dealing with?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look more carefully, item 2 is subheaded "Legality" in general terms, whereas sanitisation is one of the measures to ensure legality. "Criminal offences" implies detection of criminal offences, pursuit of criminal offences, et cetera; work on criminal offences in the broadest sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand you. What criminal offences did you at this time think had been committed? Or was it a question of you knew that criminal offences had been committed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not at all in dispute that at the time there were a lot of criminal offences. I have already shown you tables showing exactly how many, and there are lists for every crime in particular. But in this context when one insists on legality, criminal offences are a priority in terms of detecting, investigating, processing perpetrators, et cetera. So all the work related to criminal offences must be done intensively in order to ensure legality of procedure. Maybe you think that -- I simply cannot understand your thinking, your reasoning, because if you are biased or ill-intentioned, every theory can be interpreted in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, I want to give you an opportunity to interpret for us words that may be of interest for the Court in due course. If you've got nothing more to say on the meaning of crimes in that setting, let's return to page 100 that we looked at before, coming your way for speed. We looked at this in the setting of the entry towards the top of the page which says: "Remove traces of violence against property." We substituted the word "property" for "civilians," as the court will remember. But I want to look a little bit above that in this entry which speaks of "Clearing up the terrain."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Clearing up the terrain --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please ask Mr. Nice that when he is showing pages, he should do it the way he did it before, quoting the ERN number, because it is difficult to find these pages in the diary the way he's indicating them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: R0172446 for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, here, you see, we have: "Clearing up the terrain. We must know the truth. Each case must be solved. Izbica - Buha." Now, tell us about Buha. He was a PJP commander, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He was the commander of one of the PJP units, and at that point in time we assumed that he had a unit in that area, and obviously there is reference here --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not too fast. Let's just deal with it step-by-step. "We assumed he had a unit in the area." Why did you make such an assumption?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we knew roughly the area of deployment of each unit, although I did say before that, depending on the assignment, these units changed their area of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if, for example, a PJP unit had committed this dreadful massacre, the probabilities are it was Buha's unit. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the assumption that he was really there at that time. We are talking about the time when the graves were found. We are not talking about the time of the event, because let me remind you, the time of the event, as indicated in the indictment, is the month of March, and the time when the grave was found was the month of April. And the assumption here is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that he was then in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "We must know the truth."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really don't have that intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "We must know the truth. Each case must be solved. Izbica - Buha." Explain to us please how the finding of the graves is likely to solve the case and establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first thing to do is to find the graves that we saw on the aerial photograph. One cannot do anything before verifying the allegations from the aerial photograph, the satellite photograph. After that follows a number of criminal investigation steps to establish the truth. We see a case file specifying what exactly was done after the thing was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The unit of most interest to you in your effort to know the truth and solve the case would be the unit present in the area of Izbica at the relevant time, the end of March. So which unit was that and why haven't you recorded it, please?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you again: At the time when we were discussing Izbica, we had no knowledge of the event that you later described in the indictment. We were unable to think at that time about March. We were simply thinking about the facts in our possession, and the facts were that there was a grave in a certain location. In order to reach the month of March, we would have had to read the indictment. We had to read the indictment. At that moment, we did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must suggest to you, Mr. Stevanovic, you're pretty much making it up as you're going along to fit the contemporary documents.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not making anything up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then help me with this: Eventually you discover a hundred people murdered in the way we can see in the photographs. You understand it happened at the end of March. You should find the PJP unit in the area, and you should investigate. Can you take me, please, to the documents showing an investigation of the PJP unit in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said again at the end of March, and I really have to repeat that we only had information at the end of May. And you will see from the documents that investigative steps were taken somewhere near the beginning of June. And I will remind you again that I left on -- for Belgrade on the 30th of May and on the 3rd and 4th I was in Kumanovo, and until the 20th I was in Kosovo. So I did not continue to work on that case. I was instead involved with KFOR in the development of a very important technical agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You bring all these documents, you see. Let me just remind you, the NATO press statement was, I think, on the 17th of April and the matter was even discussed in a negative way on Belgrade television on the 15th, 16th of April. You could isolate the group in the area of Izbica down to the period preceding the middle of April. Now, has the police ever done that? And if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what more I need to say if you refuse to believe me that we didn't know where Izbica was until after the 20th of May. That's the only reason. We found Izbica at the end of May. The first patrol that arrived on the location found this site sometime around the 25th. I'm not sure about the exact date, but it was certainly after the 20th. And all the steps that were possible to perform were performed by the beginning of June. And we have no information whatsoever about any event taking place in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the way, was the Buha who was in charge of the PJP unit Bosko Buha who was assassinated on the 10th of June of 2002? Was that the one?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this an assassination that was ever solved by the MUP or is it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. another one that's gone on undetected?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is one of the unsolved cases, but I know that intensive investigation is underway in Belgrade in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What are the rumours as to why Buha was -- if you know of any, Buha was eliminated?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. I don't listen to rumours. I'm a professional, I've already told you, and rumours can only help in an investigation to some extent, but I'm not involved in investigations. Since 2001 I work exclusively in the police academy, I am involved in teaching and scholarly work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After the -- after the bodies were exhumed by the forces of Serbia, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information and the documentation I have, external examination, as it is termed, was performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also believe post-mortems were performed. I'm not certain enough to -- to claim that with 100 per cent certainty. I -- what was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why external examination of the bodies? You dug them up, the Serb forces, and I'm going to come back in a minute to confirm or withdraw the suggestion of the use of an excavator. So there can be no doubt about it what I'm putting: You dug them up, you examined them very briefly, in a day or so, and then what did you do with then?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the order of the investigating judge to perform an exhumation, all further steps are taken in keeping with the orders of the investigating judge. If I remember correctly, the case was referred to military investigating organs or maybe it was that experts from the Military Medical Academy were involved in the examination and post-mortems. That information was submitted to the prosecutor, and the prosecutor made a request to the investigating judge. All further action was taken pursuant to the orders of the investigating judge, and the police was only assisting the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at a map, if we can, please. It's not an exhibit yet, but it's a map of the territory with some places marked on it. You accept, don't you, that evidence of the destination of bodies has grown over time since this trial started, in particular because of the findings in Batajnica and thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the destination of the bodies found in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have that information, namely that some of the victims were found in the mass grave in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at a summary, as I suggest it is, of what happened to those bodies after they had been dug up by the Serb forces. They went to, amongst other places in the area of Izbica, they went to Suvi-Do, Mitrovica North, Supkovac, Nevolane, and Brusnik, but also they ended up in Petrovo Selo in the north and in Kladovo. Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've explained that very clearly already. I truly cannot explain why the bodies that were documented and buried in certain locations were transferred to Batajnica or perhaps Petrovo Selo. I don't know about Petrovo Selo, I haven't heard of Petrovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now, please, to look at a schedule that we've prepared. If that could be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is partly built on existing evidence and it's partly built on material that's come to light since, and will be subject to the appropriate application unless admissions can be made by the accused or those on his behalf or by any Defence witness. The document for the witness, please, first. He's got it, has he? Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at the schedule, I'll explain its format to you. It's on your right-hand side, Mr. Stevanovic. If you'd go to the last of the -- to the fifth page, you'll see the key to exhumation sites, PSII, FHH, FLP, and so on. If you then come back to the first page, you'll see how the table is formed. It gives the victims names which is according to the eyewitness who filmed, and other eyewitnesses, I think, who were present at the scene when the bodies were found. It then says - and this is in English so I'm afraid it won't necessarily be immediately clear to you - but the next column is "Victim Recovered in: Kosovo." The next entry is "Victim Recovered in: Serbia." So that looking at those, we can see that Asllan Amrushi was recovered in Serbia at PSII-17, and that's Petrovo Selo, whereas Asslan Bajra was recovered at the Suvi-Do cemetery in Kosovo. Do you understand that part of the document?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the principle involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You drew to our attention, or the accused drew to our attention through you differences between the lists of names running down the left-hand side and those who had been identified following the exhumation by Serb forces, and we see, for example, number 12 does appear in your exhibit tab 417. Looking at the bottom of the page, so does number 23. Turning on two pages, so does number 52. If you'd go to number 52. Number 54, number 67, number 73. Next page, number 86, number 103. Last page, number 109, number 113, number 115. So all those bodies, your exhumation evidence matches the name given by the witnesses giving evidence to this Court. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's come back to number 17. You see, for number 17, Dibran Dani, he was a person who was identified at the scene. He's a person who appears in the Serb lists of those they exhumed. And do you see where he landed up, Mr. Stevanovic? His body landed up in Petrovo Selo. We have the death certificates. I don't -- I'm happy to produce them, but it will take time, and we can produce them in a swifter way later. Can you explain for us, if the Court is ultimately satisfied that this is what happened, how one of the bodies at least of those the Serb forces exhumed is moved from its place of death, its place of family, to the north of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot give you an answer, and I've explained already a few times why I cannot give an answer. This really causes surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what's the distance between Izbica and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Petrovo Selo? I suspect the witness, as an experienced policeman, could give us both the -- on the -- as the crow flies and the by the road time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many kilometres or miles -- how many kilometres, roughly, from Izbica to Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 350 to 400 kilometres. This is a rough estimate, a very speedy one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And none of the roads, unless I'm mistaken, between one and the other, apart from possibly using a short stretch of the motorway, none of the roads would be other than slow-ish roads?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they're not local roads but they're regional roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The survivors who have given evidence, Mr. Stevanovic, say that excavators were used to dig up these bodies. The purpose of digging up these bodies was to hide them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would really be highly illogical. There is documentation about that, where each and every individual body was buried. There is a sketch, and if I remember correctly, there are photographs of each and every one of them too. It defies explanation, really, why this kind of documentation would be compiled, why it would remain there, accessible, public, permanent in nature, if it involved any intention of removing the bodies. This is unfounded in logic or in reason as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, if you can't help us with how it is that a body under Serb control, a corpse under Serb control, finds its way 350 kilometres by road to Petrovo Selo, can you tell us who can help us?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who did it. If you find them. I don't know who organised it. I don't know who did it. Only those who did it know. What we did at that time is what you can see here, and what somebody else did without my knowledge is something that I cannot help you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is shocking disrespect of the dead to dig them up and to transport them to places where they might not be found. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No one yet, is this right, has been identified as the transporter of the bodies from -- I beg your pardon. There's been no inquiry, is this the position, that has so far identified who drove the bodies or moved the bodies from Izbica to Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, from the moment when it was learned that there are graves in Batajnica and in Petrovo Selo, an investigation started. And again, according to the general state of information I have, this is under way, this investigation, it is under way in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By compulsion only, I suggest, of external knowledge. Let's have a look at the last question on this topic. 320, tab 75, please. My suggestion to you is the whole purpose of this movement of bodies can be shown in the first place by the callous way they were dug up. See, this is an aerial photograph taken on the 15th of May of 1999. Do you see the tractor, the trailer marks there? This is grave tampering at Izbica. Do you see the disturbance of the ground on the 3rd of June? What -- what vehicle with caterpillar tractors would be required to do a sensitive exhumation of bodies from individual graves? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see these two photographs. On the one on the right, of course, I can recognise one trace which does look like a heavy vehicle imprint, but just one, and it's obvious that it leads to this dark stain and then it goes away further. Again, according to my very lay experience, had excavators been used there would have to be more traces, or perhaps I just don't see them. There's too much of a shadow on this photograph where the grave had been, so there's nothing I can see here except for this very dark shadow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the tab number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 320, tab -- 320, tab 75. Your Honours, just give me one minute. My apologies to the Court. Before I turn from crime scenes, and I've dealt with all of them that the witness dealt with bar, I think, one. Can I make the position clear about Kotlina. His corner Judge Kwon asked me at one stage, in light of a document that had been handed over to the accused, whether all the names on the Kotlina schedule, Schedule L, were identified as coming from the KLA. At the same time, reference was made to a KLA book which is called The Phoenix of Freedom which had itself been recently served on the accused. Taking those two points in reverse order, the KLA book was served under cover of a Rule 68 letter but in fact it didn't need to be because the material is open source material, simply available in a book shop and is therefore not subject to the 68 regime but it was served out of an abundance of caution and to ensure that the accused wasn't missing something that was available to him. I think it is four of those names on the Schedule L of 17 names that appear in the book, and I think one of those names has been further confirmed by a brother of one of the deceased as being a member of the KLA. The reference to all the victims having been members of the KLA was linked to the particular disclosure made to the accused where an investigator's report spoke of them being buried at a UCK cemetery, or 12 of the 24 victims, rather, being buried at a UCK cemetery, but no names were given. So that boiling all that down, in light of all available material, four of the names appear to be the names of those credited in the book The Phoenix of Freedom as being members of the KLA. One name is also confirmed as being a member of the KLA by his brother. But the significance of entries in the KLA book is another matter for another time, but that's what all that amounts to. I may have one more question to ask about the movement of bodies later but I move now to what you've been able to tell us about Prosecution of alleged MUP offenders. Shall we look first, then, at tab 79.01, which is in the same volume, I think, volume 2. Your Honours, I suspect that this one is translated. No, 79.1. I beg your pardon. Before I develop this topic, can I remind the Court that we are still short of many translations, and there's one particular translation that I've pressed the liaison officer as one of importance, number 144, and it still isn't available. I don't know if it's maybe been translated so that I can deal with it this morning, but if not, although it will take some time we may have to just go through it because it's a potentially important document, and without a translation we will nevertheless have to deal with it. Right. We come, then, to 79.1. This document reveals a total -- if we just look at murders by MUP staff, Mr. Stevanovic, and we combine the translated part of the list with the statistics given, Your Honours will see, in the original version, and we see that murder comes, whatever it is, six or seven lines down but you can track it perhaps by its being three items after "grave incidence of robbery." That's one, two, three. And we can see that the total of murders between January and June of 1998 is one, between July and December is two, and then underneath that we have manslaughter and we see that there were two manslaughters between July and December of 1998. Is that correct, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is written in this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Neither murder nor manslaughter in the first two and three quarter months of 1999, five murders between the 24th of March and the 10th of June of 1999. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's murder and manslaughters, but to take just two famous name events, the Jashari killings and the Salihaj killings where, in the first case, maybe several members of the KLA were killed along with a large number of family members; in the Salihaj case where one member of the KLA was killed with a large number of family members, I think seven altogether including children, do those killings feature in your statistics at all? That is, the killings of people in the course of events like Jashari and Salihaj?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crimes are shown here, those that were qualified as murder. So as for the events concerning Jashari, and I cannot recall the other one that you mean, was probably qualified in a different way. Perhaps it is still in the investigation stage as conflict, as fighting, as a clash. And in this clash indeed a certain number of persons were killed, and as far as I can remember, at least one policeman was killed, perhaps even two or three policemen were killed in the clash. Probably or, rather, most certainly it was not qualified as murder. It is still in the sphere of investigation, and the investigation is supposed to show how the event concerned will be qualified. These are pure crimes here that were --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- evidently uncovered as murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm anxious not to cut you short but it has a consequence on the time that is taken. My question, I hope, is simple. Where you have women and children killed, as in Jashari, or in Salihaj, a man aged 70 and a boy aged 16, along with other family members, where that happens, the police have got to bear responsibility for what they did by way of killing these people. Now, they may be excused, but they've got to bear responsibility. Do the statistics that you've produced, does all this material that you've produced cover those killings in any way, either by showing that they've been excused or justified, that they've been investigated, or that they've simply been brushed aside and forgotten? Does this material Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cover that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material that is here doesn't cover it, but the Jashari case and what happened in that village near Srbica, there is a case file with regard to all of this. It's very similar to all of these cases, Izbica, Pusto Selo, Suva Reka, the Podujevo case. It is similar in terms of the content of the material involved. Of course I'm going to repeat this once again: This is an attack against the police, and this is a clash between the police and the citizens, and everything that happened there is certainly contained in the case file and is well documented. Investigation is still possible. I talked about the problems that we confronted in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it amount to this: That any death at the hands of the MUP that is categorised as non-criminal simply doesn't feature in the statistics at all?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's included in other statistics, in dossier A, including incidents involving loss of life. It is certainly there in terms of the number of the persons involved, but it is recorded as a single incident involving a certain number of casualties on one side and on the other side involved in the clash. The police sends its report to the prosecutor. The prosecutor decides how he is going to act and then orders the police and investigation organs what they are supposed to do. At this moment, I cannot say what was done with regard to this case, but this case, like many cases here, certainly does exist. There is a case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may return --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if it's convenient to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 77, please, Mr. Stevanovic. If you'd take it out. Tab 77. This one has been translated. It's described as "Summary of crimes against Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija between the 1st of January, 1998, and the 10th to the 20th of June, 1999." On page 1, A2, Article 47, which is murder, we see a total of 408 murders of Kosovo Albanians identified in that period. Now, your documents suggest, as we shall see, that only five of those cases could be attributed to crimes by the MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was only five. As far as I was able to note a moment ago, eight crimes. But I would like to mention this: That does not mean that mean that 408 persons were killed. The number might have been higher. There were 480 [as interpreted] acts or -- now, the number of casualties, persons that died, can be higher than this number. Perhaps that is self-evident, so I apologise if I was too lengthy in my explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What does it reveal? Does it reveal that on your case and on your statistics civilians are killing each other, or does it reveal that the military are killing civilians? What does it show?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows the number of crimes, criminal acts. And the perpetrators can, of course, come from all the structures of society. I had occasion to speak about different examples, quote different examples which speak to the fact that the perpetrators were different and the victims were different. In this case, the victims were mostly Albanians. And the perpetrators of all these acts were --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence of hundreds and thousands of people being killed and the case is that they're killed by, in large part, by the forces of the police and the army clearing people out of Albania. Are those allegations covered at all in this 408? Because if so, they haven't been investigated. You see, that's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are only 400 acts which were qualified as murder, as killings. And I've already said there were about 1.500 events involving casualties, victims, but to the present day they have not been qualified as murders, which doesn't mean that they won't be, as killings. So if any of these events, if light is thrown and these cases solved, they will be qualified as murders or the corresponding qualification pursuant to the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the prosecutions or investigations you've told us about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the impression that Mr. Nice isn't asking the question properly, putting a proper question to the witness, because the document that he refers to, if you look at page 2, it says the number of uncovered perpetrators of crimes, and then you have civilians, the police force, the active police force, the reserve police force, the army, reserve and active, and so on and so forth. All that information is on page 2 in the same table. The answers to his questions are listed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, and this is a matter that you may bring up in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the crimes you've told us about. We've dealt with Cvjetan and Demirovic. Two other points about those. First of all, Demirovic escaped to Canada; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cvjetan was eventually sentenced to 20 years, I think; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was the only one of all those offences that you can point to, I suspect, you'll confirm, charged with a war crime.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure about that qualification, but I think I have information that of late that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the only reason it was charged as a war crime was between non-governmental organisations and his own Defence lawyers insisted on its being charged as a war crime rather than a simple murder; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I don't know about that. I don't know who put forward what position in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you have information about that, I'd be interested. I think it would be useful for the Chamber to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll find it if time allows. It's in one of the tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reasons this case has come back to court, as it happens today, is because even in Cvjetan's case, despite the enormous number of people who died, his sentence was annulled in the court of appeal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about the parts of the trial and the outcome of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... something else, but while Ms. Tromp is looking for that particular piece of information, in case she can find it before I get to the next topic, just one other little detail: Did you hear the evidence in this Court given by the man Gojovic about the prosecution by the military? Did you hear or learn about that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I know is that he testified, but I didn't follow his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn, either in the press or elsewhere, of a man called Djurovic who resisted what he said was a policy of "letting people get away with it" in Kosovo and was sent, despite being a colonel in the prosecution's office, was sent back to Serbia from Kosovo? Did you learn about him?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The name doesn't ring a bell, the surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it the position that both the MUP and the army in Kosovo were pursuing the same blind-eyed approach to what was going on and making either just nominal gestures of prosecution or prosecution only when they were forced to do so by circumstances?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that isn't true, and I gave the example of great pressure and -- on the police to release detainees based on an example I know about, and the police didn't succumb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are you aware and would it surprise you to know that simply for having his name mentioned in this Court - not being a witness, having his name mentioned as a somebody who proposed proper prosecutions - Djurovic has now lost his job? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me understand this; that he would lose his job if he were to testify? Was that the sense of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His name was mentioned in this Court as somebody who favoured proper prosecution and he since then lost his job. Do you know about that? Because that shows the environment in which people still operate, I suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice -- Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm also interested in the case that went to the appeals chamber and was annulled, because I don't find it helpful just to hear that it was annulled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One needs to know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. At the moment, all I have, which is the material coming from the press report that I called for when the witness said that he had improved memory because of what he had read in the press, simply informs me that the case is to continue on Monday with witnesses because Cvjetan, sentenced to 20 years for war crimes, the supreme court annulled the sentence over appeals by attorneys and returned the case for retrial. The appeal -- the attorneys appealed because of violations of procedure and process. I can have one of my colleagues read the balance of that for detail. As to the other point that Your Honour raised, no, I haven't found the answer to it yet, but I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But we must move on, for time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next crime you told us about was the crime committed by Predrag Nikolic, Selatovic -- Zoran Djeletovic and Ivan Ivanov, the murder of the Bljakcori family. Your tabs 158 to 167, but don't get them out. Now, was that charged as an ordinary crime, not a war crime?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the criminal report was filed for the crime of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And of course charging for murder avoids the risk of a finding of war crimes which would associate superior military and political figures in the crime, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in itself, no, although once again let me repeat I cannot speak as a legal expert because according to my profession I have a lot of experience in the police, but what I learnt about is that it was an isolated case, outside any fighting, outside any combat operations or plan of any kind. A murder took place of a family in a specific place outside any unit, outside any operation or anything like that. It was murder with intent, of four policemen against a family that happened to be in that particular place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, before I conclude what I want to ask about this -- this particular crime, this point: One thing that neither you nor anybody else these days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you consider it opportune that when Mr. Nice claims something, and he claimed that some colonel was let go from his job because his name was mentioned and that a judgement was annulled and you were interested in that, that it would be necessary to say when that colonel was dismissed and when the case was annulled on appeal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice has promised to provide the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One thing that neither you nor anybody else appearing for this accused can now, I suggest to you, can now challenge, is that the lawyers Agani and Kelmendi, murdered shortly after the start of the bombing, were good men doing good work; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the name Fehmi Agani. As far as I know, he was one of the leaders of some Albanian party in Kosovo and Metohija, but I really can't recall Kelmendi. The name seems familiar, but I don't know that he was a lawyer. And I know that Agani was killed. That is incontestable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're seriously telling us as the senior policeman that you are unaware of the fact that Mr. Kelmendi and his son were taken by uniformed Serb forces from their home and murdered? You're seriously telling us that, are you? Almost one of the most famous civil rights murders in the course of this entire history and you're saying you just can remember his name? Yes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying with full responsibility that I know about the killing of Fehmi Agani, and I know that I personally wanted to hear how the investigation was getting along throwing light on that event. As to Kelmendi's murder, I can't remember any of the details, although I have it somewhere in my mind that that lawyer was killed but I can't remember where, when, or anything else related to that case. As for the killing of Agani, I do have knowledge and I was personally interested in having the matter solved. And at one point in time I thought that it had been solved parallel to the killing of the Bljakcori family, for example, and then later on it turned out that it had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, exactly. Bljakcori -- I beg your pardon. Nikolic and Djeletovic -- I beg your pardon, Nikolic and, yes, Djeletovic were both arrested for, suspected of, and apparently investigated for the murder of Agani, the man pulled from the train as he was near to -- sorry, he left the train near to his escape, going to the defence of someone else, and that investigation then was withdrawn as against these two men who were simply left to face the ordinary murder of the Bljakcori family. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I had the conviction that that matter, that case had been solved, and I think I told your investigators that. That's what I thought. But I wanted to check that out after talking to the investigators, and then looking at the case, studying the case, I established that that particular killing, the killing of Fehmi Agani was not proved during the investigation and the investigation is ongoing. The killing of the Bljakcori family was established, and that was somewhere in the same locality, as far as I recall, and it happened on the same day. That was proved. And as soon as the case was solved, four policemen were taken into custody and remained in detention until the end of the war. Afterwards, I didn't follow the developments. I also said that. And I said that we had 20 days of pressure on us from the citizenry who were convinced that it wasn't those policemen that had committed that act and that they should be released from detention, and I told them that they had never been released from custody. So that is what I know about that particular event and with respect to the killing of Fehmi Agani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The killing of individuals like the -- the large number of victims of Cvjetan, the family butchered by Nikolic and Djeletovic can be described as excesses of an individual, but is this the position, Mr. Stevanovic, that the killing at a critical time of a civil rights lawyer like Kelmendi or of an important leader like Agani can never be disguised in that way because it has a political motive and that's why those investigations have never been concluded?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. It is quite clear that the police part of the investigation and the police part of the job, if I can be more specific, in those particular cases was completed. Criminal reports were filed against perpetrators unknown of that act and all the other available evidence and proof were sent to the responsible prosecutor. That is not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. contested. I haven't got the files, but we could see, I'm sure, that the police filed a criminal report first of all with an unknown perpetrator and then with a known perpetrator in the case of the Bljakcori family. And in the case of Fehmi Agani, I'm quite sure that a criminal report was filed against perpetrator or perpetrators unknown. I really don't remember what the situation was with Kelmendi, but I'm also quite certain that what was the minimum that was done was that a criminal report was filed against perpetrators unknown, but I can't say that with certainty because I don't actually remember the entire case myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next MUP killing of which you spoke was your tabs 172 to 3, Petkovic Boban and Simic Djordje. This was tried as simple murder, wasn't it, not as a war crime?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but could you remind me what the place involved was? I can't identify the case without a place name just on the basis of the names. Perhaps it was Orahovac or Mitrovica, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Orahovac, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was also -- I think there was two criminal reports or one criminal report for the two crimes, but a criminal report for the crime of murder was filed once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That of all the crimes you've told us, is the only one that started to any extent before this accused left office, and even that one only started in June 2000; correct? When I say the crime started, the process of investigation or trial started.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were events which I had certain knowledge and I suggested that the defence prepare those cases, take those cases. Of course, there are a series of similar cases which have entered a similar stage or were completed when it was the -- was a question of civilian casualties and victims. I don't know how many more cases there are which are linked to policemen, but the statistics, of course, we do have here, and these several cases are cases on which -- about which I had a little more knowledge and information than I did compared to other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that -- the first case, the Orahovac one of Boban Petkovic and Simic Djordje was the one that was tried as murder, but the next two that you told us about, Boban Petkovic, tab 174, and Goran Veselinovic and Dragan Todosijevic, tabs 170 and 171, were never tried, were they?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. My information tells me that they were, but I can't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you can find the material to point that out to in your materials, I'd be grateful. No offence of any kind charged for expulsion at any stage as against the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course the same thing applies in relation to those as applied in relation to prosecuting people for being politicians or lawyers. Expulsion, I suggest to you, would inevitably involve a superior, and therefore you can't just charge someone at a low level and get away with it. Is that the reason no expulsions were charged?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The reason for which no expulsions had criminal reports filed was that there wasn't any knowledge of anybody moving anybody violently, forcing anybody to move, although we did consider the possibility but there was absolutely no mention of any filing or non-filing of criminal reports that depended on the affiliation of the victim or the perpetrator. So we cannot say that the killing of Fehmi Agani and Kelmendi was not prosecuted because they were lawyers. I said on several occasions that all the victims in the sense of police investigation had the same treatment, and so did all the perpetrators, regardless of their status would have been treated in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And expulsion must have been done by somebody individually had that been done. Of course, one would have to qualify the -- this conduct in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anybody prosecuted for burning other people's documents?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not quite sure. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that the evidence, and there's been a great deal of evidence in one form or another about people being kicked out of Kosovo by police, by MUP, and having their documents destroyed at the border, makes no sense because they could have applied to get their citizenship rights back. Can you point me to anybody who made that application and had it granted?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what? Granted for what, for their return? I wasn't following.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me slow it down. Your evidence is that all the accounts we've heard of people having their documents taken from them, their car licence plates taken from them and destroyed, burnt in piles, so on, is insignificant and irrelevant because those individuals could apply to the police or to the authorities and the database, a computer database, would confirm their entitlement to be treated as citizens of Kosovo. My question to you is: Can you point me to somebody who ever made such an application?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first say that my answer did not have that context at all. I did not challenge the fact that this was contrary to the law, against the law if it did happen and if it happened in any scope. And I did not say that that was not important and didn't have any meaning or sense if we had a uniform database. I just stated a fact in response to your question. I said that that couldn't be a key reason for somebody -- the main reason why somebody wasn't given citizenship. Now, with respect to the second part of your question that I don't know whether anybody filed a claim for their papers, but I'm sure cases of that kind do exist in practice, but I don't know of any such case related to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know perfectly well, Mr. Stevanovic, that by the time people have been kicked out, threatened, seen crimes on the refugees lines and so on, there's no way that they were going to apply to the same forces to come back in. You know that to be the case, don't you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the case. And it was not the case as you generalise it, that everybody was expelled and that that was the goal and so on. So I don't want to go back to that question. Departure, in most cases, was up to the people's own will, the need for them to leave an area which had become engulfed by war. So for those reasons and all the other reasons that I tried to explain in giving my answers is how things stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last three questions on killings by MUP forces, and I'm only going to deal with killings, I don't have the disposition to use time on other topics. It's right, is it, that there are just three cases where MUP have been charged with war crimes in respect of killings. One is the Cvjetan case that we've already referred to and it's back for retrial. That relates to Kosovo. The second case is the Strpce case. That's the train that runs between the border and from which people were pulled out and killed. Also called the Sjeverin case; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two cases, but they are linked in one way. Sjeverin was abduction from a bus and Strpce was abduction from a train.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In this case -- excuse me just one minute. This event happened, what, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure now. That happened in 1992. Maybe also in the beginning of 1991, but certainly in 1992. I remembered it better when I was answering questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One case certainly happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The principal killer was a known mass killer called Milan Lukic; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That kidnapping involved a group led by Milan Lukic. That kidnapping was associated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And what happened was that he was extradited, if this was something that could happen, to the body known as Republika Srpska, and from Republika Srpska he's disappeared. So he never had to face trial, did he?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember very well, he was arrested in Uzice, I believe, and detained in Belgrade, and I believe that for some procedural reasons he was released. That's what I know. But I don't know whether he was handed over or extradited or simply released. That's something I don't know at this moment. This was happening when I was involved in those activities related to the Drina, which we discussed at greater length in the previous days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was important to me was for similar incidents not to happen again, and they never happened again since I engaged my units in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, will you permit me on this occasion to make available to the witness an original of a document, it's an existing exhibit, and place on the overhead projector a copy that has got some underlinings and markings on it but I've scratched out what is relevant. This is part of Exhibit 667, tab 8. If the witness would like to have that up there, and if you would like to start there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a document exhibited in this case coming from the Supreme Defence Council, session 8, and if you look at the bottom of the page, you see the accused talking about Strpce and says: "There was just one man who conducted the control and others got on the train at the station at Strpce. One man was slipped in here and we kept looking all over. We must catch all of them. "Bulatovic: A ransom was demanded and we tried to pay the ransom for those people. Of course they were all killed. Our state security found out that Lukic's group intends to kill." Next page, please. "Our police arrested Lukic and he is behind bars. We will see what we are going to do next. We must not talk about that because we want to arrest some others too. He is a murderer and criminal." And then Bulatovic: "He is in fact a tragic figure." But enough of that. Were you aware that the senior politicians were completely in the know about who had committed the Strpce massacre at an early stage?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem logical to me that they knew because a serious massacre had happened. But I'm not aware of this meeting or the contributions that you just quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when it happened, but I know that everybody learnt about the incident itself very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what level would so-called extradition to a body like the RS have had to be referred for this man to be let go from Serbia to be tried elsewhere and then, as it happens, to disappear? To what level would that decision have to be referred? This accused?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's some level in the structure of the judiciary. I don't think that when it comes to the extradition of a national of a different state anybody else can decide. That's what I would guess, but I'm not familiar with the issues of extradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the RS --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that procedure is prescribed by the law on criminal procedure. In fact, I know it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you not aware that the RS is no state? Certainly not at that time.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot speak in terms of those categories now. Certainly Bosnia-Herzegovina is another state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, too, receive this document that was quoted a minute ago? Mr. Nice said the 8th session of the supreme --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let a copy be passed to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I explained to Your Honours, I was seeking your leave to use it just by showing it on the overhead projector. But perhaps he can have the original and I could have the English copy back. Then I'm content to work that way. That's the original, the B/C/S to the accused; the English copy back to me. Thank you very much. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Few small points that I want to deal with -- and I take it we still don't have an English translation of Exhibit 144. It hasn't arrived. You told us at an early stage that you were unaware of the Red Berets being formed in 1991, later -- later to the JSO. You suggested to us that what had happened at the anniversary meeting in 1996 must have been different from what happened at the video meeting in 1997. Let me be quite clear about this, Mr. Stevanovic: I'm suggesting to you that was a complete lie by you and I suggest that can be proved by the following: You confirmed last week that your superior Djordjevic was present and could be seen on the Kula video from 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djordjevic can be seen at the ceremony in Kula in 1998, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... his deputy, associated with him freely.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not his deputy ever. Only one in my career was I deputy of the head of a police sector. Djordjevic and I were appointed assistant ministers --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the same procedure. He was head of sector, but we were both assistant ministers and I was never his deputy.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe in his function of head of police sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that your proposition that somehow the -- Frenki Simatovic put on a different display and gave a different history in one year from the history he freely gave to people, including your colleague then, or your peer, Djordjevic the following year is ridiculous and is something that you've been obliged to say because you're trying to hide your knowledge of the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true. I am not trying to obscure what I know. I remember very well that I was invited to the ceremony to mark the establishment of the unit for special operations. Of course, I don't remember every detail of every speech, but my entire recollection of that ceremony indicates that that unit was established then or the day before, but the ceremony was dedicated to the establishment of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next point relates to tabs 82 and 83. I needn't ask you to look to them. They're both dated mid-April, I think, of 1999, and they deal with the movement of civilians. Do you accept, as we have heard from Exhibit 234, the UNHCR Neill Wright, that by the 5th of April the cumulative refugee total was some 400.000? Do you accept that figure?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you this moment whether I accept this figure. Of course by that date there had been significant movements of civilians and a significant number of civilians had left Kosovo and Metohija. Every day MUP was informed of the rough number of people who had crossed the border, and I have recollection of the number of 8.000 people in total -- 800.000 people in total who had left Kosovo and Metohija during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My suggestion to you is that orders of the type that you -- we looked at in 82 -- tabs 82 and 83 were cover-up orders that it would be easy to draw -- easy to draft once the majority of people had been kicked out and that they are just that, cover-up.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
