utterances.text: I don't know the dates on those orders, but I believe they are contemporaneous, and I assert what I have been asserting all this time; the leadership of all police units and military units as well were very concerned over this and did whatever they could to stop the movement of civilians in any way apart from using force. And I can tell you that after the beginning of NATO bombing, that day was the -- on the agenda as a great problem every day. However, there was no way to stop the movement of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except by using force, and that would probably have been a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 3, Exhibit 144, which we don't have translated. No. It must be tab 4, beg your pardon. Binder 4. We see --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid I really -- it's very difficult to deal with this document in the circumstances and I just simply, knowing that it was top of the priority list, did not allocate my unlimited resources to getting it translated when it would have been translated twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But this document, just tell us again in a sentence what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we quoted from parts of this document, and we can see from the title what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although of course this name, "Operative intra-departmental staff for combatting terrorism" is unfamiliar to me as a concept. But from the group of people who attended, one can conclude that it is the name of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused called the meeting, did he?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems logical, but I was invited to this meeting by the minister of the interior, not the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see all the top officials, political and military and police there, don't we? Djordjevic, Milosevic, Milutinovic -- Milutinovic, Sainovic --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- everybody is there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what proposal?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to refresh my memory. Yes. The conclusions are on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Continuation of the Joint Command." Is that one of the proposals?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I read something to that effect. One of the conclusions was that, a Joint Command only in the sense that I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any more documents exist of the same kind of meeting that this one is evidence of?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I'm not aware of other documents related to the meeting that is recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll have to deal with that document when it's translated through later witnesses. You were promoted to the rank of general by this accused?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was promoted by the president of the Republic of Serbia, in keeping with the then law on ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The police were regarded as paid very favourably in comparison with the army?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact data that was in my possession I'm unable to quote. I knew that the police was paid appropriately to the problems they had to deal with. Whether they had salaries higher than those in the army and what the ratio was, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that -- was that the point of your question, Mr. Nice, to say that they were more highly paid than the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the suggestion, or the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I read one passage where it says, Don't tell the armies they are paid less. I don't remember the tab number at this moment. Do you remember, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One fact indicates that, but it was not about salaries. Those were compensations paid for tours in Kosovo, and since those compensations were regulated by a variety of regulations, the police had higher compensations or, in other words, per diem, but that was compensation for tours of duty outside the basis of their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Military ranks were given partly because Badza wanted it but partly because it reflected the developing extreme militarisation of the police force of which you were a member; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say, first of all, that those were not military ranks. We can talk about ranks that had the same names as military ranks. There is a law governing ranks for police members. I don't know the exact name of that law. So we cannot talk about military ranks. We can only talk about names and terms used for police ranks that are similar to those of military ranks. And I believe I also explained in great detail that the existence of ranks does not mean militarisation, because rank is not the source of powers, duties, authorisations. It is the law that vests certain powers --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the individual, not the rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there. And as a matter of history, is it right that the Constitutional Court of Serbia subsequently found that the accused had acted unconstitutionally in doing what he did about the ranking system for the police?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was some provisions of that law that were declared unconstitutional, and I don't need to tell you that the president of Serbia did not pass laws. We know very well who passed laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Couple of other things and then one more short topic to which we must return. As a matter of fact, simply as a matter of fact, two of the ministers of the interior who would have lain between the accused and people below him, Stojiljkovic and Sokolovic, both committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, after the wars were over, you, Djordjevic, and Lukic were all honoured to the same degree by this accused; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was to the same degree or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but it was together with another thousand policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Order of the Yugoslavian Flag First Class, you, Djordjevic, and Lukic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you won't believe me, but I don't know the exact name of that order. I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were entirely to be trusted by the leadership from the moment of your promotion to general, and indeed before, and Srebrenica is the proof. Remember you told us about what you did at the border and my suggestion to you that you knew and had to know what was coming and going through that border? Remember that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you said, indeed, and I replied to that, and I have to repeat my answer; namely, that I had nothing to do with the events in Srebrenica nor do any units under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've seen -- sorry. As you drove -- as you escorted DutchBat out, do you remember being held up by Serb tanks, or by tanks, in any event, that were themselves passing from Republika Srpska into Serbia proper? Remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a Dutch colonel called Franken. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember an officer of that name. I would have thought it was a general. But if you remind me, I will tell you whether it is the same person or not. I remember a Dutch general, grey haired, tall. I knew his name at the time, but I can't -- it eludes me for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I probably got his rank wrong. Then that's him. I'm not suggesting he's given evidence in this Court of what I'm suggesting to you, but I'm suggesting that in his sight and at the departure of the Dutch from Srebrenica or from Bratunac, so far as you were concerned, there were sights of departing tanks, and you must have seen that as well.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am absolutely certain that I didn't see any tanks on the way to or from Bratunac. I said Bratunac was two kilometres away, but it's not even that. It could be a kilometre from the bridge across the Drina. I cannot tell you exactly, but I know it's very close to the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I want to return to a topic, last couple questions. By the time you were down there in Bratunac, the killing had happened, or nearly all of it had happened, and as we've seen from the video, on a wide scale. From code cables we've got passing between Yugoslavian bodies in New York, Washington, and no doubt in Belgrade, seven days before you were sent there there was knowledge of the disappearance and probable fate of Muslims from Srebrenica. Now, I'd like you to look, please, at a video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I would have to answer first."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Needs to have the screen at a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to see you in this video. Can you, by the way -- we've stopped the frame at the picture of the bearded man. Can you tell us who he was or who he is?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't remember the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us who the man to his right and our left, wearing the dark glasses, is.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see him well enough, and I cannot recognise anyone from this image.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have a more complete image maybe.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Thank you for your hospitality. We will see each other there. Good-bye. "Good-bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where are you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's me, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Good-bye. All right. All the best to you. Good-bye. My best to you." This was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Play it once more because I want to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Gentlemen --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is when DutchBat was being handed over by Mladic, they having been hostaged for a week or so, to you. Thousands already killed and with Belgrade being in possession of information for over a week that things were going badly, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover]... to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who is that man to your right? Did he come down to you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I can identify him now. It is General Mile Puzovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What part of the services did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- he belonged to the public security sector, and I believe at that moment he was head of the department of border police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Where did you pick him up then, or did he travel independently?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We travelled together. He and I travelled together to Bratunac. We had the same assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So he would have had access to the leadership as well as access that you also had to Mladic; yes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I did not have access to Mladic. Mladic was there where we had gone to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This man, the man on the right there with the grey hair, who is he?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to take a look again. I didn't see him. I have to see. I do not recall anybody else arriving with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That man there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot recognise this man. I really can't. I don't know this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You coming from Belgrade were all trusted to deal with Mladic. Were you told not to ask any questions?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you not even yourself at that time concerned to know what had happened to the people who had been clearly at his mercy with the Dutch being his hostages for over a week? Were you not interested to know that, as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you're getting me involved in a story that I have nothing to do about. That is one of my many assignments, truth to tell, a very delicate, a special one, but one of the many assignments that I received and that I carried out. May I remind you that as far as Srebrenica is concerned and what happened in Srebrenica, my units took 800 soldiers of the BH army, and they were perfectly fine. Nothing happened to them. That is proof of how we treated anyone who tried to cross the border, even soldiers of the BH army. This was a specific task, a specific assignment that I got from my superior to ensure safe passage to the Dutch Battalion through Serbia. I did not know any of what you're saying or could I infer from this conversation any of that. Since this was a general from the Dutch Battalion, it was only natural for someone who was at his level to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, from the police, if there can be any --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... subject only to this, Your Honour: The answers to the documents, of course, are not with the witness at the moment. We don't know if and when they'll come through. Likewise any answers he may have further about the film. But that's all I wish to ask him. Can we deal with exhibits tomorrow? Or at the end of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps at the end of re-examination. We will adjourn now and resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of June, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
